newsitem.title: UK: Scandal hits Hong Kong over immigration boss.
newsitem.headline: Scandal hits Hong Kong over immigration boss.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten said on Wednesday that the British colony's immigration department had not been tainted by a scandal surrounding its former head, who resigned last July.
"We have got no reason to believe that the integrity or security of the department have been affected in recent years," Patten told reporters after meeting British Prime Minister John Major.
The Hong Kong government admitted earlier on Wednesday that Laurence Leung quit as Immigration Director after a graft probe uncovered misconduct.
Patten said it was vital that Hong Kong's civil service should maintain the highest standards of integrity.
"We had reason to believe in the case of Mr Leung that these standards were certainly not being met," he said.

In Hong Kong, government personnel chief Lam Woon-kwong told a Legislative Council inquiry the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) investigated Leung to see if he had breached a law against bribery.
He said the probe failed to substantiate suspicions of criminal offences but raised grave questions about Leung's integrity.
"The ICAC investigation has uncovered information which causes us to have great doubt on Mr Leung's suitability to remain in the service," Lam said.
He read out to the inquiry a draft letter written months ago mentioning disciplinary questions and noting Leung used a HK$1.76 million (US$228,000) government housing loan to buy property in Canada.
Lam's unprecedented statement marked a U-turn in the government's public stance on the case. Leung and the government initially said he retired for "personal reasons".
But Leung, testifying at the inquiry last week, backtracked and said he had been forced to resign.

Leung, 55, who spent seven years as head of immigration and 31 years in the Civil Service, held a highly sensitive post, with strong security implications in the delicate period running up to China's takeover of the British colony on July 1.
He was responsible for areas such as the issuing of passports and visas, immigration and border controls and was privy to sensitive information in handover talks with China.
